sources.title: Modern Library Top 100: board novels and nonfiction lists
sources.note: Examined both complete lists of 100 titles. The nonfiction list includes James, Whitehead/Russell, Rawls, Moore, Dewey, Berlin and Popper as well as history, memoir, criticism and science.
sources.location: Nonfiction board list, positions 1–100; factual extraction research/_runs/2026-09-13/compilation/S02-modern-library.json
candidates: The Open Society and Its Enemies
sources.limits: English-language twentieth-century selection; editorial board perspective is not a global or reader consensus. Novel and nonfiction positions belong to separate lists.

targets.P: Philosophical authors explicitly represented by named philosophical books in the board nonfiction list: James, Whitehead/Russell, Rawls, Moore, Dewey, Berlin and Popper. This supports candidate reception, not a poll ordering of philosophers.

sources.title: 100 must-read classics, as chosen by our readers
sources.note: Reader recommendations and editorial descriptions produce a broad classics selection.
sources.location: Relevant introduction, selection, or discussion excerpts; full page review is not asserted.
sources.limits: Publisher-curated and commercially linked; shares ownership with Modern Library.

targets.N: Reader-selected list explicitly includes In Cold Blood, Travels with Charley, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, Lark Rise to Candleford and The Art of War. Nonfiction candidates only; fictional titles are not reassigned.

sources.title: Confucius
sources.note: The Analects transmits multiple representations of Confucius. The entry treats ritual, virtue and family-state relations while warning that later traditions select different aspects of his legacy.
sources.limits: Authorship and doctrine are historically underdetermined; no single modern label captures all reception.

targets.N: The Confucius article supports the Analects as an influential philosophical nonfiction text; compilation and attribution remain qualified.

sources.title: Laozi
sources.note: Daodejing's ethical, political and spiritual interpretations differ. The text's influence is broad, but the existence of its traditionally named author is disputed.
sources.limits: Do not infer an established historical individual from a surviving named text.

targets.N: The Laozi article supports the Daodejing as philosophical literature rather than a prose novel; traditional attribution remains qualified.

sources.title: Nāgārjuna
sources.note: Emptiness and arguments against intrinsic nature shaped Buddhist philosophy across Asia; the entry distinguishes reliably attributed works from later name-attributions.
candidates: The Fundamental Wisdom of the Middle Way
sources.limits: Dates and attributions are uncertain; verse treatises need complete-work eligibility review.

targets.N: The Nagarjuna article supports his fundamental Middle Way treatise as philosophical nonfiction; preserve translation and interpretation uncertainty.
